summary:
La Guajira is a department of Colombia and stands under the national framework, which is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, a route that replaced the earlier practice in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025.

The sharpest risk in La Guajira comes from armed groups rather than the statute. Since March 2024 armed actors in the department have circulated flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". A visibly trans visitor operating in an area where named kill lists are posted faces a documented threat from groups outside state control.

Lethal violence is recorded nationally as well. On 5 April 2025 a video circulated showing Sara Millerey, 32, flailing in a creek outside Medellín in Bello, Antioquia, unable to swim with fractured legs, arms and hands, before she drowned; her mother Sandra Borja said "They killed her for being who she was," and President Petro ordered an urgent investigation. Thirteen trans people were killed in the first quarter of 2025, the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025, and more than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023.

Entry and partner recognition work in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016 and the National Registry issued a memo directing all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office.

Access to premises and to detention is governed by court order and administrative decree. Constitutional Court judgments T-314 of 2011 concerning the Tequendama Hotel, T-909 of 2011 concerning guards at the Cosmocentro mall in Cali and T-301 of 2004 concerning police at the Santa Marta boardwalk protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees.

Protection machinery exists without having closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience.
tangentialFactors:
Reporting on 6 August 2025 by CNN's 'As Equals' project found that the viral Millerey video shocked the country but that killings continued under armed gangs, framing being queer in parts of the country as "to sign your own death sentence". The finding is national rather than departmental, and it describes the atmosphere a visitor to La Guajira would enter.

The territorial pattern of armed-group campaigning is best documented in another department. In Caquetá, The Guardian reported on 30 July 2024 that armed groups ran a "social cleansing" campaign, with flyers on the street and via WhatsApp naming "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets. A trans woman and local election candidate was told by three armed men she had one week to leave town, hid for a week, then fled at night; a second trans woman said a friend had been killed. Trans salon owner Tatiana Cespedes was forced to move twice after death threats from armed men, and trans women in the department have few options beyond sex work. Caquetá is one data point illustrating the wider pattern, not a description of La Guajira.

Countrywide figures for the same period show eight trans women killed between February and April 2024 and 41 in 2023. Killings of queer Colombians continued after the Millerey case, described in reporting as calculated brutality persisting amid the country's decades-long civil conflict.

Social climate is a compounding factor. Colombian society is described in national sources as generally conservative on LGBT issues, and an October 2019 Invamer poll reached 50% support for same-sex marriage for the first time, with 47% opposed. Neither figure is department-specific.
localsOnly:
Residents change the sex marker on identification by signing a document before a notary, without psychiatric or physical evaluation, a route available since the rule change approved in June 2015; the right to legal gender change itself dates from 1993 and does not require surgery. Identification documents began carrying "trans" and "non-binary" markers in November 2025. A comprehensive trans law remained under legislative consideration in 2025.

Consensual same-sex activity has been legal since 1981. Congress passed a law banning discrimination based on sexual orientation in 2011. Same-sex marriage has been available since the Constitutional Court's April 2016 ruling, which made Colombia the fourth Latin American country to do so, and same-sex couples have had full adoption rights since 2015. Transgender people have been permitted to serve openly in the military since 2015.

Institutional obligations are set by decree. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree established procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, healthcare, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

Conflict-related accountability runs through the Special Jurisdiction for Peace, which in July 2023 indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities; the UN Human Rights Committee noted concern.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory carries no La Guajira-specific finding on policing, prosecution of the flyers, healthcare provision or access to facilities; the departmental profile source yielded nothing usable and the Caquetá reporting explicitly contains no La Guajira-specific finding. Those gaps are unresolved rather than confirmed as either protective or hostile.

No source states whether the November 2025 "trans" and "non-binary" document markers are in routine issue through registry offices in La Guajira, or how the notary route performs in the department's rural and indigenous-counsel territory.

No department-level data was sourced on killings of trans people in La Guajira itself, on displacement caused by the March 2024 kill-list flyers, or on any protective response by the Attorney General's Office or the military to those specific threats.
